title: Ladder
pitch: An agent calls a tool on your page. Ladder runs it against a copy first, shows the person who owns the records what will change, lets them cut it down, then commits under a guard that rolls back.
about_excerpt: An agent calls a tool on your page. Ladder runs it against a copy first, shows the person who owns the records what will change, lets them cut it down, then commits under a guard that rolls back. Like Comment Story Updates Before WebMCP the tool ran on a server and the operator stood outside the room. With WebMCP it runs in the tab they already have open. The guarded path: fork and record, proof, cut down, then replay the same execute() under a guard that rolls back. A tool wrote a field the proof never showed. Requested 27, applied 0, refused 27, and the agent is told to replan. Four tools on the page. Two read, two write. Only the writes take the fork-and-proof path. The same engine on a second product: edge infrastructure rollout, built in a day, with no shipment anywhere in it. What Ladder is A human control plane for consequential WebMCP actions. WebMCP gives agents the ability to act on websites. Ladder gives humans the ability to decide exactly what those actions are allowed to change. Before an agent changes real data, Ladder runs the exact same tool against a clone of the page's state, records every write, and turns them into a proof the human can edit. The human approves or narrows it. Ladder then reruns the same tool against real state under a guard, and anything outside the approved proof rolls the entire commit back. Why this matters WebMCP settled how an agent acts on a page: a tool is registered, the agent calls it, the page does the work. That is the hard part and it is solved. What it did not settle is what happens when the agent is wrong. The operator sees a function call and a name. A call that is ninety per cent right can only be taken whole or thrown away whole. Freight operations run on legacy systems built around human operators: screens, workflows, permissions, manual decisions. The next generation of these systems will be AI-native. Agents will search records, propose actions and execute operational workflows directly. That creates a new problem. How do humans and agents collaborate when an agent can change the operational system itself? An agent may correctly identify 27 shipments that need a remedy, and the right answer is almost never "do all 27". One carries lithium-ion batteries and cannot go on a passenger flight at all. One has twelve hours of temperature-control endurance left and cannot wait until morning. One is ordinary freight whose customer will not notice. The operator needs to apply that judgment to the agent's proposal without taking the whole task back by hand. As legacy operational software becomes AI-native, the interface between human judgment and agent autonomy becomes part of the operating system itself. Ladder is a pattern for building that boundary. The freight story below is the proof, not the identity. What it does Ladder executes the same WebMCP tool twice: once as a shadow transaction, once as the guarded commit. The shadow run calls the tool's real execute() against a structuredClone of the page's state, behind a Proxy that records every write. Nothing real is touched. What the tool would do becomes a diff. The person sees the blast radius: how many records, how much money, how many of the actions are irreversible, and a bar showing that share against the whole dataset. They untick what they do not want, and every figure moves as they do it. The button they press says "Apply 20 · Refer 4 to duty manager". Then the same execute() runs again, against real state, through a Proxy that lets the approved writes through, silently skips the ones that were narrowed out, and throws a ScopeViolation if the tool goes anywhere the preview never showed. A violation rolls the entire commit back. The developer writes one function, the way they already do. Ladder runs it twice. Nothing disappears into "success" One run, accounted for end to end: Agent requested: 27 Above the operator's authority, referred: 4 Left for the operator to decide: 23 Operator removed: 3 Applied: 20 Every requested action is accounted for. applied plus every rejected count equals requested on every path the app can reach, including the ones where nothing lands. There is a test for it. What people and agents can now do together The person's edit reaches the agent as data it can act on. When someone cuts 27 down to 20, the tool does not return "success". It returns what actually happened and why the rest did not: { "status": "partially_applied", "requested": 27, "applied": 20, "rejected": [ { "reason": "the operator removed these from the change", "count": 3, "ids": ["HAWB-70003", "HAWB-70005", "HAWB-70007"] }, { "reason": "above the gateway operator's authority, referred to a duty manager", "count": 4, "ids": ["HAWB-70001", "HAWB-70002", "HAWB-70023", "HAWB-70025"] } ], "replan_required": true } Different refusals carry different reasons and the agent can tell them apart. A row the tool itself declined comes back with the rule that declined it. A record the person removed comes back as its own bucket. A record that changed while they were deciding says so. The agent is never left guessing which kind of no it received, so it can ask again about the four only instead of re-proposing all twenty-seven. Autonomy works the same way. After a run of clean approvals Ladder drafts a standing rule with caps and an expiry, and a person ratifies it the way they would approve a pull request. A person can also set one up front. When a rule is ratified, Ladder calls unregisterTool() and re-registers the tool with a description that states the rule, so the agent's own toolset changes as trust is granted . When the rule expires, the tool reverts. Irreversible tools can never carry a rule at all. The case it was built on Thursday, 19:40. A flight from Frankfurt to Chicago is cancelled. Two consolidations were on it, so 42 shipments belonging to 31 different customers are now unbooked. Nobody assembled that list. The cancellation did. There are ninety minutes to the first cutoff, and three ways out. Rebook on the same carrier tomorrow morning, which is free and costs eighteen hours. Put it on a competitor's freighter tonight, which recovers the time and costs money. Truck it to another airport and fly from there, which lands one day late instead of two. The person responsible has to decide which shipments are worth which remedy, against consequences, in the ninety minutes they have. How we built it React, TypeScript and Vite. Two products ship from one engine to prove the engine is not the domain: index.html . Air freight recovery. Four tools: search_shipments and get_shipment read, propose_remedy and notify_customers write. edge.html . Edge infrastructure rollout. Four tools: list_pops and inspect_pop read, roll_config and page_oncall write. Eight tools across two pages. Neither product's engine knows what a shipment or a POP is. The second product took a day. That is the evidence that the engine is an engine. The core is about 900 lines. runShadow() forks state with structur
video_transcript_excerpt: Frankfurt to Chicago is cancelled. 42 shipments, 31 customers, one operator to rebook them. The first move is not a right. It sets what she is looking at. Two of the 42 carrying lithium batteries. No record change and none was hidden. And one click gives it back. This is ladder. When an agent calls a tool on your page, the person who owns those records sees what is about to change and keeps only what they want. Before Web MCP, the tool ran on a server somewhere else. It could reach the records, but the person answerable for them only found out once the change had landed. Web MCP moves it into the page she already has open. Under the session she is already signed in with. She is in the room when the change is proposed. Four tools handed to the browser by the page. Two only read. The other two are reviewed. Now, the right. The agent proposes a remedy for everything on console A. Ladder runs a tool for real, but against a copy of the page. 27 shipments matched. Four cost more than she may sign off. Refuse the whole call and you lose the 23 that were right. She unticks three. Every figure moves with her and the stamp goes from apply 23 to apply 20. Here is what the agent gets back. Not success. 20 applied. Three she removed. Four waiting on a duty manager. That adds up to the 27 it asked for and every refusal names its IDs. The agent reads that and asks again about those four only. Neither side started over. The duty manager gets a sheet with four rows and signs it. The receipt says no re-plan is needed. A tool can also be wrong. This one is made to write a field that was never on the proof. Ladder rolls the whole commit back and the record is exactly as it was. The engine does not know what a shipment is. Same code, different product. 36 edge sites, 23 go out, six are closed by a rule, seven need a traffic lead. Ladder is a guard, not a sandbox. A tool that goes around it is not covered. Tested in Chrome with web MCP enabled and in chat GPT's built-in browser. Web MCP lets agents act. Ladder lets people decide what those actions are allowed to change.

live_observation.first_impression: A polished explanatory landing page presents Ladder as a human-control layer for consequential agent actions, with tabs for the problem, related work, and proof.
live_observation.action_attempted: Tried opening the THE PROOF tab.
live_observation.after_state: The initial snapshot exposed the proof tab and proof links, but the subsequent browser interaction returned no usable interactive elements and no changed state was captured.
live_observation.notes: The page visibly explains fork, proof, cut-down, replay, and guarded rollback behavior, including a partially applied example.
